problemSolved: Represents an end-user or external service initiating an HTTPS request to an application hosted in the OpenShift cluster.
interactions: Sends HTTPS requests to the cluster's public Route hostname.
Receives TLS certificate presented by the HAProxy ingress router.
explorationCommands:
# Simulate a request from outside the cluster
curl -v https://<route-hostname>/api/endpoint

problemSolved: The central control plane component that exposes the Kubernetes/OpenShift API. All cluster mutations (Pod creation, config changes) pass through it, providing authentication, authorization, and admission control.
interactions: Receives all kubectl / oc commands and REST API calls.
Writes cluster state to etcd and notifies controllers via watch events.
Validates and persists resource objects before they are acted on by other components.
explorationCommands:
# Check API server health
oc get --raw /healthz

# List all available API groups
oc api-resources --verbs=list --namespaced -o name

problemSolved: Watches for unscheduled Pods and assigns them to nodes based on resource availability, affinity rules, taints, and tolerations. Ensures workloads are distributed efficiently.
interactions: Watches the API Server for Pods with no assigned node.
Evaluates node capacity (CPU, memory) before binding a Pod.
Writes the scheduling decision back to the API Server as a binding object.
explorationCommands:
# View scheduler logs
oc logs -n openshift-kube-scheduler -l app=openshift-kube-scheduler --tail=50

# Describe scheduling events for a pod
oc describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> | grep -A5 Events

problemSolved: The node-level agent that runs on every worker node. It watches the API Server for Pods assigned to its node, then instructs the container runtime (CRI-O) to start, monitor, and stop containers accordingly.
interactions: Polls the API Server for PodSpec updates for its node.
Calls the CRI (Container Runtime Interface) to manage container lifecycle.
Reports node and Pod status back to the API Server.
Mounts volumes and applies cgroup resource limits.
explorationCommands:
# Check kubelet status on a node
systemctl status kubelet

# View kubelet logs
journalctl -u kubelet -f --no-pager | tail -50

problemSolved: A lightweight container runtime implementing the Kubernetes CRI (Container Runtime Interface). It pulls images, creates containers using OCI-compliant runtimes (runc/crun), and manages the container lifecycle on behalf of kubelet.
interactions: Receives gRPC calls from the Kubelet via the CRI protocol.
Delegates container process creation to runc or crun.
Calls CNI plugins to set up container networking (netns, veth, IP assignment).
Sets up cgroup v2 hierarchies for resource enforcement.
explorationCommands:
# List running containers managed by CRI-O
crictl ps

# Inspect a specific container
crictl inspect <container_id>

# View CRI-O logs
journalctl -u crio -f --no-pager | tail -50

problemSolved: The OpenShift ingress controller, running as an HAProxy instance. It watches Route objects and dynamically updates its configuration to proxy external HTTP/HTTPS traffic to the correct backend Services and Pods.
interactions: Terminates TLS using certificates stored in Secrets or provided by cert-manager.
Re-encrypts or passes through traffic depending on the Route's TLS termination policy.
Forwards traffic to ClusterIP Services which load-balance across Pod endpoints.
explorationCommands:
# Check router pods
oc get pods -n openshift-ingress

# View HAProxy config inside the router pod
oc exec -n openshift-ingress <router-pod> -- cat /var/lib/haproxy/conf/haproxy.config | head -60

# View route object
oc get route <route-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml

problemSolved: The Open vSwitch integration bridge managed by OVN-Kubernetes. It is the central virtual switching fabric on each node. All pod veth interfaces and the host uplink connect to this bridge, and OVN flow rules govern how packets are forwarded between them.
interactions: Connected to all pod veth pairs on the node.
Receives OpenFlow rules from the OVN controller specifying forwarding logic.
Handles local pod-to-pod traffic without leaving the node.
Encapsulates inter-node traffic using Geneve tunnels.
explorationCommands:
# List all interfaces on the OVS bridge
ovs-vsctl show

# Dump OpenFlow rules for the integration bridge
ovs-ofctl dump-flows br-int | head -30

# View OVN logical switch ports
ovn-nbctl show

problemSolved: One end of a virtual Ethernet pair (veth). Each pod gets a veth pair: one end lives inside the pod's network namespace (as 'eth0'), the other end lives in the host's root namespace and is plugged into the OVS bridge. This is how traffic crosses the namespace boundary.
interactions: Peer interface resides inside the Pod's network namespace as eth0.
Host-side end is attached to the OVS br-int bridge as a port.
Created and managed by the OVN-Kubernetes CNI plugin during pod startup.
explorationCommands:
# List veth pairs on the host
ip link show type veth

# Find which veth belongs to a specific pod (match by peer index)
ip link | grep -A1 'veth'

# Show bridge ports
bridge link show

problemSolved: Provides network virtualization and isolation. It gives each Pod a private routing table, IP address, and packet filtering space, preventing port conflicts on the host.
interactions: Attaches to a host-side veth pair to bridge traffic out of the namespace.
Provisioned and configured by the OVN-Kubernetes CNI plugin during pod creation.
explorationCommands:
# Step 1: Find the target host PID of the container process
crictl inspect <container_id> | grep pid

# Step 2: Enter the isolated network namespace using the PID to view interfaces
nsenter -t <PID> -n ip addr show

problemSolved: Enforces CPU, memory, and I/O resource limits and accounting for each container. Prevents a single runaway container from starving other workloads on the same node.
interactions: Hierarchy is created by CRI-O/runc when the container starts.
Kubelet monitors cgroup usage to report resource consumption back to the API Server.
OOM killer is triggered by the kernel when a container exceeds its memory limit.
explorationCommands:
# Find cgroup path for a container
crictl inspect <container_id> | grep cgroupsPath

# View memory limits from the cgroup
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/<cgroup_path>/memory.max

# View CPU quota
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/<cgroup_path>/cpu.max

problemSolved: The actual application process running as PID 1 inside the container's PID namespace. It is the leaf node of the entire Kubernetes ownership chain — the workload the entire infrastructure exists to run.
interactions: Runs inside the intersection of a Network Namespace (netns), cgroup slice, and PID namespace.
Receives inbound socket connections on its private IP address.
Writes logs to stdout/stderr which are captured by the container runtime.
explorationCommands:
# Execute a shell inside the running container
oc exec -it <pod-name> -n <namespace> -- /bin/sh

# View the process tree inside the container
oc exec <pod-name> -n <namespace> -- ps aux

# Check what port PID 1 is listening on
oc exec <pod-name> -n <namespace> -- ss -tlnp
